target_customer: Companies that need part-time security, privacy and compliance experts but cannot hire full time
problem: Cybersecurity talent was scarce and expensive; small firms could not afford full-time senior security staff.
business_model: marketplace with a 20 percent success fee on hired worker compensation, later fractional CISO and compliance services

founders.name: Ken Baylor
education: law degree, MBA and Ph.D. (institutions not stated)
founders.background_notes: YC launch post of 16 March 2016 says he was a CISO for over 10 years and holds a CISSP. Source: https://ycombinator.com/blog/stealthworker-yc-w16-is-a-marketplace-for-talented-cybersecurity-specialists

technical_complexity.rationale: A matching marketplace and vetting process; no hard technology.

defensibility.rationale: Staffing marketplaces are easy to copy; value rests on a network of vetted experts that can be poached.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No incumbent action found; the market shifted to vCISO consulting firms that sell the same fractional model.

market_need_then: eWeek in May 2016 reported companies getting creative to relieve a shortage of security professionals, naming the virtual CISO as the most popular Stealth Worker service.

identity.voice_and_tone: professional services, states it is not a law firm

brand_strength.rationale: Searches found no press or community about the brand; the name collides with unrelated stealth startups and security guard firms.

pivots.from: marketplace of part-time security contractors with a 20 percent success fee
pivots.to: small firm offering fractional CISO, DPO and AI governance services
pivots.why: not stated; inferred from comparing the 2016 YC post and the current site

outcome_analysis: Stealth Worker launched from Winter 2016 as a marketplace for part-time security experts founded by a former CISO, took a small seed amount and never announced a larger round. It remains a five-person firm selling fractional CISO, privacy and AI governance services, with no acquisition or shutdown found. The outcome looks like a small services business rather than a venture-scale marketplace, but the cause of limited growth is not public.
notes: Competition empty: the YC post names none and no competitor dated near 2016 was found; the eWeek and Dark Reading articles (search summaries only, Dark Reading blocked with 403) do not name rivals. The $120K figure comes from CB Insights and Caplight aggregators which disagree on co-investors (AltaIR Capital and Three Tree Ventures vs 408 Ventures) and date (16 vs 22 March 2016); treat as unverified. Pivot row is an inference from site comparison, flagged as such.
